chat.author: Shraddha Hegde
chat.text: @Andrew Stone If you make it optional on the transit you have the opportunity to pick what is programmed in the forwarding plane.Its really a corner case but I don't see why the signalling draft has to strictly mandate something not leaving any options to change based on issues found during deployment

chat.author: Andrew Stone
chat.text: @Sharaddha my concern is the entity doing the compute did so assuming a specific SID would be selected to achieve the given TE and behavior for that specific instruction. I guess I just have trouble seeing where you would want to do hop-by-hop steering but be okay with omitting doing a SID selection based on the same value you did the TE compute.

chat.author: Shraddha Hegde
chat.text: The SID being selected at the transit is based on the ERO computed so there is no hop-by-hop steering being done. All the discussions are around if there are multiple SIDs satisfying the same ERO which one is being picked.

chat.author: Shraddha Hegde
chat.text: Its possible adj-sid changed from the time of compute while RSVP reservation request arrived at the transit

chat.author: Andrew Stone
chat.text: if it's signalling for an SRv6 plane wouldn't the ERO just be the corresponding SID  (ipv6 address) anyways?

chat.author: Shraddha Hegde
chat.text: @Andrew Stone, Ipv6 address and the END.X/uA sid are different. uA sid can be dynamically allocated or statically configured based on operator choice

chat.author: Andrew Stone
chat.text: true, okay so in the SRv6 case basically saying let the ERO compute using the interface addresses, on signalling, then let the node decide the sid

chat.author: Italo Busi
chat.text: I my experience, when talking to people outside of the TEAS WG (outside IETF but also within IETF), things that we think are "well-known" are actually well-known to us but not to a broader community

chat.author: Vishnu Beeram
chat.text: Dhruv, Thanks for the pointers! We already reference those documents in the draft. What we found, however, is that the discussion of auto-bandwidth mechanisms—both for individual tunnels and for multiple tunnels grouped into a container—is scattered across several documents. The intent of this new draft is to bring these pieces together and provide a cohesive, authoritative document within TEAS that explains how distributed bandwidth management works and why it represents a valid and viable architectural approach.

chat.author: Boris Khasanov
chat.text: Thanks!
